t: Check If Word Is Valid After Substitutions — Editorial
o: A string is valid if it can be built by repeatedly inserting "abc" anywhere. Equivalently, we can *reverse* the process: a valid string must contain "abc" as a substring, and removing any occurrence of "abc" must again yield a valid (or empty) string. So s is valid iff we can repeatedly delete occurrences of "abc" until nothing remains. In Example 1, "aabcbc" contains "abc" at index 1; removing it leaves "abc", which removes to empty — valid. In Example 3, "abccba" contains no "abc", so it is immediately invalid. With length up to 2·10⁴, an O(n) or O(n log n) simulation easily fits; the key is to avoid quadratic repeated scanning.
k: Validity is equivalent to being able to erase every 'abc' substring until the string is empty.
A stack processes this in one pass: whenever the top three characters form 'a','b','c', pop them.
Any leftover characters on the stack mean the string is invalid.

a.i: Directly simulate the reverse operation: find any occurrence of "abc", delete it, and repeat. If we end with an empty string, s is valid; if at some point no "abc" exists but the string is non-empty, it's invalid. This mirrors the problem statement exactly and is easy to reason about, though naive rescanning can be slow in the worst case.
s: While s is non-empty, search for the first occurrence of "abc".
When s becomes empty, return true.
a.t: O(n²) worst case — each removal costs O(n) to rebuild the string, and there can be up to n/3 removals.
a.sp: O(n) for the working copy of the string.

a.i: Process characters left to right with a stack. Whenever the top of the stack holds 'a' then 'b' and the current character is 'c', those three form a complete "abc" unit — pop them. This greedily matches innermost insertions first, which is always safe because removing any "abc" from a valid string keeps it valid. If the stack is empty after processing everything, s decomposes fully into "abc" units.
s: Initialize an empty stack (or use the input array as the stack).
For each character ch: push it onto the stack.
If the stack has at least 3 elements and its top three are 'a','b','c', pop all three.
After processing all characters, return whether the stack is empty.
a.t: O(n) — each character is pushed once and popped at most once.
a.sp: O(n) for the stack in the worst case (e.g., "aaa...abc...bc").

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force deletion idea briefly, then present the stack solution as the optimal one-pass answer. Pitfalls: forgetting that only the exact sequence 'a','b','c' may be popped (order matters), strings whose length isn't a multiple of 3 are automatically invalid (the stack check handles this naturally), and inputs like "abccba" fail because no 'abc' ever forms. Edge cases: single characters (invalid), "abc" itself (valid), deeply nested patterns like "aaabbbccc" (valid). A likely follow-up: generalize to inserting an arbitrary pattern p — the same stack technique works by checking the top |p| characters against p each step.
